analysis.one_liner: Bars Congress from delegating lawmaking power to federal agencies, voiding rules not written by Congress itself.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Homeland Security Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal law to prohibit Congress from delegating 'legislative power' to the President, federal agencies, courts, or anyone else. Every rule, penalty, or regulation binding the public would have to be written in full by Congress itself in a statute; anything else would have no force, and individuals could sue to block enforcement. It would also have required the Government Accountability Office to report which existing laws contain delegations, with the stated goal of phasing them out.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and individuals who face federal regulations — environmental limits, financial rules, workplace standards, health and safety requirements — would gain, because rules not fully spelled out in an Act of Congress would become unenforceable. People who believe Congress has improperly handed lawmaking to 'unelected bureaucrats' would get a constitutional reset: every binding rule would need an affirmative vote of both chambers and the President's signature.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any Act of Congress from delegating legislative powers to the executive branch, the courts, agencies, states, or any other entity, and voids any statute that does [S2][S3].

No new rule, regulation, presidential directive, or adjudicative decision regulating the public could take effect unless authorized by a compliant Act of Congress, and noncompliant ones would have 'no force or effect' — with no civil or criminal action able to be brought under them [S2][S3].
Any person aggrieved by executive branch action under a noncompliant law could sue the United States for relief, including an injunction blocking enforcement, reviewed de novo [S2][S3].
The Comptroller General would have to report to Congress identifying all statutes containing prohibited delegations, so they could be phased out [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the loss of the protections that agency rulemaking delivers: food and drug safety standards, environmental limits, financial and consumer rules, and workplace safety requirements are written in detail by agencies under authority Congress delegates. Congress cannot realistically write every detailed rule itself, so most such rules would become unenforceable within 90 days of enactment, and entire statutes with delegations would be stripped of effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal regulations

drawbacks.text: The bill denies force or effect to any noncompliant Act of Congress and bars any legal or regulatory action under it — meaning major statutes that depend on delegated rulemaking could stop functioning 90 days after enactment [S2][S3].

Congress cannot write detailed technical rules at the volume modern government requires; stripping agencies of that role would leave many areas — from pollution limits to banking rules — without enforceable standards [S3].

The bill reaches delegations to states and 'any other organization or individual,' which could invalidate cooperative federalism programs and grant-condition regimes that ordinary state and local governments administer [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill advances a genuine constitutional theory — that Article I vests all legislative power in Congress — and would make every binding rule traceable to elected lawmakers, with an individual right to sue. But its mechanism is abrupt and sweeping: within 90 days, virtually the entire federal regulatory system, which carries out protections Congress wrote in broad terms on purpose, would lose force. The realistic trade is more congressional accountability in theory for far weaker health, safety, environmental, and financial enforcement in practice.

outcome.mechanism: Rand Paul introduced it in November 2013, the Senate sent it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the 113th Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the Write the Laws Act on November 7, 2013 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the House before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The regulatory status quo continued unchanged: federal agencies kept their rulemaking power, and regulated industries remained subject to the existing framework rather than gaining the blanket unenforceability this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the existing regulatory system

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Write the Laws Act and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, which sat in the committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so there was no recorded partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would strip agencies of the power to write rules and penalties binding the public, voiding any delegation. Agencies' loss of power and the public's loss of regulatory enforcement are intertwined — the same action.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, financial firms, energy, pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: Rules not fully written by Congress would become unenforceable, relieving companies of compliance burdens across environmental, financial, and safety law. That gain comes directly at the cost of the protections ordinary people rely on.
